common_name: Stella de Oro Daylily (Classic Compact Reblooming Golden Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Stella de Oro was the breakthrough cultivar that popularized reblooming, compact daylilies and remains one of the most widely sold perennials in North America.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Introduced in 1975, Stella de Oro was a landmark cultivar that produced golden-yellow, ruffled 2.75-inch flowers continuously from late spring through frost rather than the single few-week bloom flush typical of older daylilies, and its compact size and toughness made it an instant favorite for commercial landscaping as well as home gardens. It tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and poor soil with equal ease, needing only routine deadheading of spent scapes to keep it tidy, and clumps can go many years between divisions. Because it has been planted so extensively, some gardeners now seek out newer reblooming cultivars for variety, but its reliability and near-constant color still make it a dependable low-maintenance choice for borders, mass plantings, and roadside beds.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rozanne blooms almost continuously from late spring until frost with essentially no deadheading required, unlike most hardy geraniums that flower in a single flush.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2008, Rozanne is widely considered the best hardy geranium ever introduced, producing large, violet-blue, white-centered flowers almost nonstop from late spring through the first hard frost, far surpassing the brief single bloom flush typical of most cranesbill geraniums. The sprawling, mounding habit weaves attractively through and under other perennials without being aggressive, and the plant is sterile, so it never becomes weedy from self-seeding. In the heat of a zone 9 summer it appreciates afternoon shade and consistent moisture to keep flowering strong; otherwise it needs almost no care beyond an occasional light trim to keep the mound tidy.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Walker's Low is sterile and mildly aromatic, discouraging deer and rabbits while drawing bees in large numbers, and shearing it back hard after the first flush produces a strong rebloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Named Perennial Plant of the Year in 2007, Walker's Low forms a broad, billowing mound of soft gray-green, aromatic foliage topped with airy spikes of lavender-blue flowers over an exceptionally long bloom season from late spring into fall. Despite its name it grows considerably taller and wider than the name suggests, and shearing the whole plant back by about a third after the first big flush of bloom keeps it tidy and triggers vigorous reflowering. It is highly drought-tolerant once established, rarely troubled by deer or rabbits thanks to its pungent foliage, and one of the most reliable long-season bee and pollinator plants for a sunny border edge.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Matrona's sturdy, dark-tinted stems resist the flopping that affects many taller sedums, especially in richer soil.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Matrona is a stately upright sedum with thick, dusty-mauve stems and gray-green, purple-tinged succulent foliage that make it an attractive structural presence even before it blooms, topped in late summer by broad, flat clusters of soft pink flowers that age to a rich rusty-bronze and stand through much of the winter. Its sturdier stems hold up better in wind and rain than many older upright sedum cultivars, especially when grown lean rather than overfed. Left standing over winter, the dried flower heads and stems add structure to the dormant garden and offer shelter for beneficial insects, and the clump can be divided every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Jeana Garden Phlox (Highly Mildew-Resistant Pollinator Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Jeana was discovered growing along a Tennessee riverbank and shows outstanding natural resistance to powdery mildew, the disease that disfigures most garden phlox by midsummer.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade with good air circulation. Found growing wild along the Harpeth River in Tennessee, Jeana has become one of the most celebrated garden phlox introductions of recent decades for its outstanding resistance to powdery mildew, a fungal disease that routinely turns the leaves of older phlox cultivars gray and unsightly by midsummer. It produces unusually large numbers of small, soft lavender-pink flowers packed into wide domed clusters over a long summer bloom season, and research trials have documented it as an exceptional magnet for butterflies, drawing more pollinator visits than most other phlox cultivars tested. Divide the clump every few years in spring to maintain vigor, and keep soil consistently moist for the best flowering.
sources: Mount Cuba Center Trial Garden Report — Phlox paniculata
